tasks.after: Average 44.5, lowest 38, highest 52, standard deviation about 4.2 (all in ₹ thousand). ₹54,000 is about 2.2 standard deviations above the average, so it is unusual, but it is one day. Before crediting the layout, check whether yesterday was a weekend, a salary day or a festival, and watch the next week or two. If most days stay high, the layout probably helped.

reflection.prompt: When have you seen a survey or “study” quoted that you now doubt? What would you want to know about how it was done?
reflection.hint: How many people, who were they, and who chose them?

quiz.title: Opt in, or random?
quiz.scenario: A Kanpur online pharmacy wants to test a new checkout page. A manager suggests showing it only to users who opt in, and comparing them with users who don’t.
quiz.question: Why should users be assigned to the two pages at random instead?
options: So the test finishes sooner, because nobody has to stop and choose which page to see
So both groups end up with exactly the same number of users every day
So users can’t pick a page, which would break the app’s terms of use
So the groups are alike except for the page, and a difference can be credited to it
quiz.explanation: Users who opt in may be keener or more used to the app, so they could buy more anyway. Random assignment spreads those differences evenly, so a gap between the groups comes from the page.
quiz.why_wrong: Random assignment doesn’t make a test faster; it gives groups of roughly equal size, not exactly equal every day; it is there to make the comparison fair, not to follow any terms of use.
quiz.learning_outcome: Random assignment is what makes a test fair.

quiz.title: Two app ratings
quiz.scenario: App A shows 4.9 stars from 40 reviews. App B shows 4.6 stars from 52,000 reviews.
quiz.question: Which statement is most defensible?
options: App A is clearly better, because its rating is higher and recent reviews matter more
Both are equally reliable, because a star rating is an average either way
App B’s rating is the more reliable estimate; App A’s could change a lot with more reviews
They can’t be compared at all, because the apps have different numbers of reviews
quiz.explanation: With 40 reviews a few new ones can move the average a lot; 52,000 reviews pin it down closely.
quiz.why_wrong: A higher average from 40 reviews can’t show A is better; reliability depends on how many ratings sit behind each average; the different review counts are exactly what tells you which to trust more.
quiz.learning_outcome: Small samples give uncertain results.

quiz.title: The early winner
quiz.scenario: A team checks its A/B test every hour, and stops it on day 2 because the new design is ahead by 9%.
quiz.question: What is the main risk?
options: Early leads swing by chance; stopping at the first good moment often crowns a false winner
None: a 9% lead after two days of traffic is enough to be confident the new design is better
Two days is too short for the servers to show both designs to a large enough number of users
Checking every hour slows the website down and changes how users behave
quiz.explanation: Results swing a lot early on. Checking constantly and stopping when ahead almost guarantees you’ll catch a lucky moment.
quiz.why_wrong: A two-day lead can be pure chance; showing two designs isn’t limited to a certain number of days; checking results doesn’t change what users see.
quiz.learning_outcome: Fix a test’s length before it starts.

quiz.title: The satisfied members
quiz.scenario: A gym chain surveys members who have just renewed, and 90% say they are “very satisfied”. The CEO wants “90% of our members are very satisfied” in an advert.
quiz.question: What is the problem?
options: 90% is too high to believe; honest satisfaction surveys of gym members rarely go above 70%
The survey needed more questions, about equipment and trainers, to measure satisfaction properly
Advertising rules allow survey results only when an outside agency ran the survey
Only members who renewed were asked; those who left are missing, so it overstates satisfaction
quiz.explanation: Asking only people who stayed leaves out those who left: a selection bias that flatters the result.
quiz.why_wrong: A high number can be true for the group asked; more questions don’t fix who was asked; the problem is the sample, not who ran the survey.
quiz.learning_outcome: Check who was left out of a sample.

workbook.hook: Every number wobbles. Statistics tells you when a wobble is news.
idea: Numbers move around even when nothing has changed. Standard deviation measures the usual wobble, and a value more than about 2 standard deviations from the average is unusual.

A survey is a sample, with a margin of error that narrows as the sample grows. But a bigger sample doesn’t fix who chose to answer. Only a random A/B test, planned before it starts, shows that a change caused a difference.
why: You stop celebrating or panicking over one good or bad day
You know how far to trust a survey result
You can show that a change worked, not just hope it did
workbook.simple: Think of your daily commute. Some days take 35 minutes, some 45. One 50-minute day doesn’t mean the road has changed. A month of 50-minute days does.

myth.wrong: A bigger survey is always a more trustworthy survey.
myth.right: A bigger sample narrows the margin of error, but if the wrong people answered, 5,000 replies still mislead. Who answered matters as much as how many.

example.title: The cloud kitchen’s busy Saturday
example.body: Imagine Neha, who runs a cloud kitchen in Thane. Over 4 weeks her daily orders average 120, with a standard deviation of 10. One Saturday she gets 128: less than 1 standard deviation above average, an ordinary day. The next Saturday she gets 148, nearly 3 standard deviations above. Now she checks why, and finds a cricket final was on that night. She notes the reason before hiring more staff.

terms.meaning: The ordinary ups and downs in a number when nothing has really changed.
How far a typical value sits from the average. =STDEV in Google Sheets.
The people or rows you measured, out of all you could have.
The range around a sample’s result where the true figure probably lies. It is usually given at 95% confidence: 95 times in 100, the true figure is inside it.
When the people who answer differ from those who don’t.
A random split into two groups at the same time, to see if a change makes a difference.

try_it.title: Is today unusual?
try_it.prompt: A college canteen sold these numbers of samosas on 8 ordinary days: 210, 195, 230, 205, 220, 190, 215, 200. Today it sold 260. Work out the average and the sample standard deviation, and say how many standard deviations above the average 260 is. Is it unusual? What would you check before calling it a trend?
try_it.look_for: An average of about 208, a standard deviation of about 13, and 260 about 4 standard deviations above the average.
try_it.check: Paste the 8 numbers into Google Sheets and use =AVERAGE and =STDEV. If the AI’s numbers differ from yours, trust the sheet. Even an unusual day is one day: check for an exam, a fest or a holiday.

try_it.title: How wide is the range?
try_it.prompt: A poll of 100 students finds 60% want the library open on Sundays. Roughly what is the margin of error at 95% confidence? What would it be with 400 students? In two sentences, explain why the bigger poll is narrower, and what it still can’t fix.
try_it.look_for: About ±10 points for 100 students and about ±5 for 400: four times the sample halves the range. It should add that size doesn’t fix who chose to answer.
try_it.check: Try a free online margin-of-error calculator with 100, then 400, at 95% confidence. Then ask yourself: if only keen library users filled in the poll, would 400 replies help?

workbook.tip: Write down the test’s measure, length and size before it starts, and don’t pick a winner until it ends.
workbook.mistake: Comparing people who chose the new thing with people who didn’t, and calling the difference the effect.

checks.scenario: A bakery in Ranchi sells about 300 buns a day, with a standard deviation of 20. On Tuesday it sold 315.
checks.question: How should the owner read Tuesday?
options: A clear rise, since 315 beats the usual 300
A worrying sign the usual pattern is breaking
The start of a trend, if Wednesday also beats 300
An ordinary day, within one standard deviation
checks.hint: How far is 315 from 300, measured in standard deviations?
checks.why: 315 is 15 above the average, less than one standard deviation of 20, so it is ordinary noise. It isn’t a clear rise or a broken pattern, and about half of all ordinary days beat 300, so two in a row is no trend.

checks.scenario: A poll of 150 Pune commuters has a margin of error of about ±8 points.
checks.question: Roughly what would it be with 600 commuters, chosen the same way?
options: About ±2 points
About ±4 points
About ±6 points
About ±8 points
checks.hint: What does a bigger sample do to the range, and how fast?
checks.why: 600 is four times 150, and four times the sample halves the range, so about ±4. ±2 would need sixteen times the sample, ±6 assumes the range shrinks only a little, and ±8 ignores the bigger sample.

checks.scenario: A café chain in Bengaluru runs an A/B test of a new menu board from Monday to Friday of one week only, with customers split at random.
checks.question: What is the main risk?
options: Five days give each group too few visitors to split
Weekend customers behave differently and aren’t in it
Running on weekdays makes the random split unfair
A new menu board needs a month before anyone notices it
checks.hint: Which customers could the test never see?
checks.why: Weekend visitors, such as families and groups, may choose differently, so a weekday result may not hold all week. Running two full weeks covers both. A busy café gets plenty of visitors in five days, the random split is fair on any day, and customers see a menu board at once.

modules.title: Python and pandas for analysis
modules.summary: Load, clean, filter, summarise and join data with pandas in a free Google Colab notebook, and check each step.
modules.outcome: Clean and summarise a real CSV file with pandas in a notebook, checking the row count and totals at each step.

learn.title: Why Python, and where to run it free
learn.body:
Python repeats your steps exactly on next month’s file. It handles millions of rows, and a notebook records every step so anyone can rerun it. pandas is Python’s table library. A DataFrame, usually called df, is a sheet you can program.

Run it free in Google Colab (colab.research.google.com) with a Google account. There is nothing to install. A laptop or a college computer is easier than a phone. Free sessions can stop when idle; if that happens, run the cells again from the top. Python in Excel also exists, but it needs a paid Microsoft 365 plan.

Worked example: your first cell.
import pandas as pd
df = pd.read_csv("https://myskills.org.in/practice-data/masala-mart/orders.csv")
df.shape
The output (2030, 9) means 2,030 rows and 9 columns. df.head() shows the first 5 rows, and df.info() shows each column’s type and blanks.

learn.title: From file to answer
learn.body:
A whole small analysis: a Hyderabad tiffin service’s file payments.csv has 4 rows:
txn_time,customer,amount,status
02/05/2026 08:10,R1,120,success
02/05/2026 13:05,R2,150,failed
03/05/2026 08:20,R1,120,success
05/05/2026 19:30,R2,150,success

df = pd.read_csv("payments.csv")
df["txn_time"] = pd.to_datetime(df["txn_time"], format="%d/%m/%Y %H:%M")
ok = df[df["status"] == "success"]
ok.groupby("customer")["amount"].sum()
Output: R1 240, R2 150.

Why format=? 02/05/2026 could be 2 May or 5 February. format= says exactly which, and stops with an error if a row doesn’t fit. dayfirst=True only prefers day-first; it is not strict.

The common mistake is letting pandas guess. Read month-first, 02/05/2026 becomes 5 February. Always look at a few converted dates with df.head() before you go on.

To bring in another table’s columns, merge on a shared key:
areas = pd.DataFrame({"customer": ["R1"], "area": ["Kondapur"]})
df = df.merge(areas, on="customer", how="left")
how="left" keeps every payment, like a LEFT JOIN. R2 has no match, so its area is NaN, pandas’ blank. Leave how= out and only matching rows stay.

learn.title: Filter, clean, then check
learn.body:
To filter on two conditions, use & for “and” and | for “or”. Put brackets round each condition:
df[(df["status"] == "success") & (df["amount"] > 5000)]
Python’s word and gives an error on whole columns, and so does leaving out the brackets.

To change values in matching rows, use df.loc[df["amount"] < 0, "status"] = "check". The older form df[df["amount"] < 0]["status"] = "check" never changes df in pandas 3 (January 2026). Colab may run an older pandas, so check pd.__version__.

To clean: df = df.drop_duplicates() removes rows identical in every column. subset="customer_id" compares only that column, so it would also delete every repeat order.
To turn “₹1,250” into a number:
df["order_value"] = df["order_value"].str.replace("₹", "").str.replace(",", "").astype(int)

After each step, compare df.shape and a total with the step before. If either grows after a merge, rows were duplicated, like a fan-out in SQL.

tasks.title: Clean and summarise the raw export
tasks.prompt: Open a new notebook in Google Colab and load the messy export: df = pd.read_csv("https://myskills.org.in/practice-data/masala-mart/orders_raw.csv"). Then: drop exact duplicate rows; turn order_date into dates with format="%d/%m/%Y"; turn order_value into numbers (remove "₹" and commas with .str.replace, then .astype(int)); merge in category from https://myskills.org.in/practice-data/masala-mart/products.csv with how="left". Finally, filter to kept orders (returned == 0) from April to June 2026, and total order_value by category, largest first. Report that table and df.shape after each step.
tasks.hint: Check yourself: after dropping duplicates you should have as many rows as orders.csv. After the merge, 58 rows have no category (new SKUs). If the filter gives an error, look for a missing bracket.
tasks.after: df.shape goes (2065, 9) on loading, (2030, 9) after drop_duplicates, (2030, 9) after the date and value changes, and (2030, 10) after the merge, with 58 rows that have no category. The April to June kept orders (458 rows) total: Masala blends ₹51,680, Whole spices ₹49,440, Ground spices ₹44,140 and Gift boxes ₹9,687.

tasks.title: Read the code, then run it
tasks.prompt: Read this code and explain each line in plain words. df = pd.read_csv("https://myskills.org.in/practice-data/masala-mart/orders_raw.csv") / before = len(df) / df = df.drop_duplicates(subset="customer_id") / print(before - len(df)). Now run it. How many rows did it remove? Then reload the file and run df.drop_duplicates() with no subset instead. Which version removes only true duplicates? What would the other do to a revenue total?
tasks.hint: A customer who orders three times appears in three rows. Is that a duplicate?
tasks.after: Line by line: load the raw file, store its row count, drop every row that repeats a customer_id (keeping each customer’s first row), and print how many rows went. It removes 1,590 of the 2,065 rows, leaving one row per customer. Plain drop_duplicates() removes only the 35 rows identical in every column: the true duplicates. The subset version throws away every repeat order, so revenue would fall sharply.

reflection.prompt: What repetitive data task would you most like to automate? List the steps a script would follow.
reflection.hint: Anything you do every week in the same order is a candidate.

quiz.title: Totals by city
quiz.scenario: A Jalandhar sports-goods seller has loaded its orders into a DataFrame df with the columns order_id, city and value.
quiz.question: Which line gives the total order value for each city?
options: df.groupby("city")["value"].sum()
df.groupby("value")["city"].sum()
df["value"].sum() / df["city"].nunique()
df.pivot("city", "value").sum()
quiz.explanation: groupby makes one group per city; selecting "value" and summing gives each city’s total.
quiz.why_wrong: Grouping by value and summing city mixes up the two columns; total value divided by the number of cities is one average, not a total per city; this df.pivot call stops with an error and wouldn’t add anything up anyway.
quiz.learning_outcome: groupby plus an aggregate summarises by category.

quiz.title: The dairy’s monthly file
quiz.scenario: A Kolhapur dairy sends a delivery log every month. Its date column is written day first, such as 05/04/2026 for 5 April 2026. The owner wants the code to stop with an error if any row doesn’t follow that pattern, instead of guessing.
quiz.question: Which line should you use?
options: pd.to_datetime(df["date"], dayfirst=True)
pd.to_datetime(df["date"], format="%d/%m/%Y")
pd.to_datetime(df["date"], format="%m/%d/%Y")
pd.to_datetime(df["date"], errors="coerce")
quiz.explanation: format="%d/%m/%Y" says exactly how every date is written, so 05/04/2026 becomes 5 April. pandas stops with an error at any row that doesn’t fit.
quiz.why_wrong: dayfirst=True only prefers day first: if the first date is 04/13/2026, pandas can read every date month-first, with only a warning; %m/%d/%Y puts the month first, so 05/04/2026 becomes 4 May; errors="coerce" never stops, and quietly turns dates it can’t read into blanks (NaT).
quiz.learning_outcome: Give pandas the exact date format, so a bad row stops the code.

quiz.title: Orders with unknown customers
quiz.scenario: A Dhanbad electronics store runs orders.merge(customers, on="customer_id", how="left"). A few orders have a customer_id that isn’t in customers.
quiz.question: What happens to those orders?
options: They are kept, with the customer columns empty (NaN)
They are dropped, because they have nothing to match in customers
The merge stops with an error naming the missing customer_ids
They are matched to the nearest customer_id that does exist
quiz.explanation: A left merge keeps every row of the left table; unmatched rows get NaN in the right table’s columns.
quiz.why_wrong: Dropping unmatched rows is what an inner merge does; pandas doesn’t raise an error for keys with no match; a merge only matches equal keys, never a “nearest” one.
quiz.learning_outcome: Choose the merge type for the rows you must keep.

quiz.title: Big successful payments
quiz.scenario: A Gwalior payment company has a DataFrame df of transactions, with status and amount columns.
quiz.question: Which line keeps only successful transactions above ₹5,000?
options: df[(df["status"] == "success") & (df["amount"] > 5000)]
df[(df["status"] == "success") and (df["amount"] > 5000)]
df[df["status"] == "success" & df["amount"] > 5000]
df[(df["status"] == "success") | (df["amount"] > 5000)]
quiz.explanation: pandas combines conditions on whole columns with & for “and”. Each condition needs its own brackets, so each comparison is worked out before & joins them.
quiz.why_wrong: Python’s word and can’t combine whole columns, so it raises an error; without brackets, & is applied first, to "success" and the amount column, which raises an error; | means “or”, so it would also keep failed transactions above ₹5,000.
quiz.learning_outcome: Combine pandas conditions with & and brackets.

workbook.hook: Do the steps once in Python, and next month’s report takes a click.
idea: pandas is Python’s table library, and a DataFrame (df) is a sheet you can program. Google Colab runs it free in a browser with a Google account, and the notebook records every step.

Read dates with an exact format=, filter with & and | and brackets round each condition, and merge tables on a key with how="left". After every step, compare df.shape and a total with the step before.
why: The same notebook reruns on next month’s file in seconds
It handles files far too big for a spreadsheet
Every step is written down, so others can check it
workbook.simple: A pandas notebook is like a written recipe. Working in a spreadsheet by hand is cooking from memory: fine today, but next month you can’t be sure you did the same steps.

myth.wrong: You need to install Python on a powerful computer before you can start.
myth.right: Google Colab runs pandas free in a browser with a Google account. A laptop or college computer is easiest, but there is nothing to install.

example.title: The mobile shop’s monthly report
example.body: “Can you redo last month’s numbers for this month too?” asks Imran’s cousin, who runs a mobile shop in Aurangabad. Imran tracks its sales from a CSV file. In Colab he writes four lines: read the file, convert sale_date with format="%d/%m/%Y", keep rows where status is "paid", and group by brand to sum the amount. df.shape shows 1,240 rows before the filter and 1,198 after. Next month he changes only the file name and runs it again.

terms.meaning: pandas’ table, usually called df: a sheet you can program.
A free online notebook for running Python in a browser.
The number of rows and columns, such as (2030, 9).
Splits rows into groups so you can sum, count or average each one.
Brings in columns from another table on a shared key, like a SQL join.
pandas’ blank: a missing value.

try_it.title: Predict the output, then run it
try_it.prompt: Explain each line of this pandas code in plain words, and tell me the exact output: import pandas as pd / df = pd.DataFrame({"team": ["Red", "Blue", "Red", "Blue", "Red"], "points": [10, 7, 4, 12, 6]}) / df.groupby("team")["points"].sum()
try_it.look_for: Blue 19 and Red 20, with Blue listed first, because groupby sorts the team names.
try_it.check: Open colab.research.google.com, put the three lines in a cell (one per line, without the slashes) and run it. If the AI’s totals or order differ from Colab’s, Colab is right.

try_it.title: Which line changes the table?
try_it.prompt: I want to mark every negative amount as "check" in the status column of a pandas DataFrame. Which of these two lines works, and why? A: df[df["amount"] < 0]["status"] = "check" B: df.loc[df["amount"] < 0, "status"] = "check" Give me a 4-row DataFrame with amounts 200, -50, 120 and -10 to test it on.
try_it.look_for: Line B works. Line A sets the value on a temporary copy, so df doesn’t change.
try_it.check: Run both in Colab on the 4 rows and print df after each. Only line B should turn the two negative rows to “check”. Your Colab may also show a warning for line A.

workbook.tip: Print df.shape after every step in a notebook. One number per step catches most silent mistakes.
workbook.mistake: Letting pandas guess a date format, so 02/05/2026 can become 5 February without any warning.

checks.scenario: After df = df.drop_duplicates(), a hostel mess’s df.shape goes from (2065, 9) to (2030, 9).
checks.question: What changed?
options: 35 rows were removed
35 columns were removed
9 duplicates were removed
Nothing, as the columns match
checks.hint: Which of the two numbers moved, and what does it count?
checks.why: df.shape shows rows, then columns. The first number fell by 35, so 35 duplicate rows went. The 9 columns are unchanged, and the columns staying the same doesn’t mean the rows did.

checks.scenario: Before a merge, df.shape is (900, 5) and the amount column totals ₹2.1 lakh. After the merge it is (900, 7), with the same total.
checks.question: What does this show?
options: Some rows were duplicated in the merge step
Some of the rows were dropped in the merge
The merge failed and changed nothing
Two columns came in; no rows multiplied
checks.hint: Compare the rows, the columns and the total before and after.
checks.why: The row count and the total are unchanged, so nothing was duplicated or dropped. The column count rose from 5 to 7, so the merge did bring in two columns.

checks.scenario: Every month, Leela gets a new export of about 500 sales from a shop and repeats the same 12 cleaning steps by hand in a spreadsheet.
checks.question: What is the main gain from writing the steps in a pandas notebook?
options: It runs much faster than a sheet on 500 rows
The steps rerun exactly on next month’s file
It works out which cleaning steps are needed
It can open file types that Sheets can’t
checks.hint: What stays the same from month to month?
checks.why: A notebook records the steps, so they rerun the same way on each new file. 500 rows is quick in a sheet too, Leela still decides the cleaning steps, and a sales export opens in Sheets already.

modules.title: Dashboards people use
modules.summary: Choose the right chart, design a dashboard around decisions, build it with free tools, and check any number a tool drafts.
modules.outcome: Build a one-page dashboard that shows key numbers against targets, where the problem is, and what changed.

learn.title: Pick the chart for the question
learn.body:
Match the chart to the question.
- Change over time: a line chart.
- Comparing categories: a bar chart, sorted largest first.
- Part of a whole: a stacked bar, or a pie with only two or three slices.
- Two numbers together: a scatter plot.
- Exact values: a well-formatted table.

Common mistake: a bar chart whose axis doesn’t start at zero. Worked example: three stores sold ₹100 lakh, ₹101 lakh and ₹102 lakh. If the axis starts at ₹99 lakh, the bars are 1, 2 and 3 units tall. ₹102 lakh now looks three times ₹100 lakh, though it is only 2% more. Bars must start at zero.

A pie with nine slices is another trap. People can’t compare angles well, but a sorted bar chart shows the order at once.

learn.title: A dashboard answers three questions
learn.body:
A good dashboard page answers three questions, from top to bottom.
1. Are we on track? Key numbers against their targets.
2. Where is the problem? A breakdown by city, centre, channel or product.
3. What changed? A trend against earlier periods.

Worked example: a coaching chain with 6 centres in Nagpur, Indore and Raipur.
- Top row: admissions this month, 412 against a target of 450. Fees collected, ₹38 lakh against ₹40 lakh.
- Middle: a sorted bar chart of admissions by centre. Centres below target are red; the rest are grey.
- Bottom: a line chart of weekly admissions for the last 12 weeks.
The area head sees at once that 2 centres are behind, and calls them.

Put the most important number top left. Keep each page to one purpose. Use colour only to point at what needs action.

learn.title: Build it free
learn.body:
You can build a dashboard free in three ways.
- Looker Studio (lookerstudio.google.com): free in any browser. Connect it to a Google Sheet, then add scorecards, charts and filters. It is easiest on a laptop.
- Google Sheets charts: Insert > Chart. They work on a phone too, and are enough for a simple one-page view.
- Power BI Desktop: free on a Windows computer, and used by many employers in India. It has no Mac or phone version.

In Power BI you write measures in DAX, its formula language. For example:
Return rate = DIVIDE(SUM(Orders[returned]), COUNTROWS(Orders))
Every chart reuses the measure, so the number is the same everywhere.

Copilot in Power BI can draft measures and pages. It is a paid feature some employers provide. Whatever drafted a number, check it against a total you trust before you share it.

tasks.title: Build Masala Mart’s dashboard
tasks.prompt: Build a one-page dashboard for Masala Mart’s founder from orders.csv, loaded into a Google Sheet as in Module 2 (Spreadsheets that answer questions). Use Looker Studio connected to your Sheet, or Google Sheets charts; Power BI Desktop is fine if you have Windows. Include: three key numbers for September 2026 against their targets (revenue, target ₹85,000; orders, target 200; return rate, target under 5%); a sorted bar chart of revenue by city; and a line chart of monthly revenue from October 2025. Submit a link or a screenshot, and one sentence on what the founder should act on.
tasks.hint: Check your September revenue against a SUMIFS or pivot total before you share. Colour only the numbers that miss their target. Does the line chart show the Diwali season?
tasks.after: For September 2026: revenue ₹81,581 against ₹85,000 (missed), 195 orders against 200 (missed), and a return rate of 4.1% against under 5% (met). The sorted city chart starts with Mumbai, Bengaluru and Delhi. The monthly line peaks in October 2025, the Diwali season. A good action sentence names the gap: revenue and orders are just short of target while returns are fine, so the founder should focus on winning more orders.

tasks.title: Fix a bad chart
tasks.prompt: A colleague shows Masala Mart’s revenue by city as a 3D pie with 10 slices. Make that pie yourself in Google Sheets from a pivot of revenue by city, then redraw it as a better chart. Which city is third, and how easy was that to see in each chart? Write two sentences on why your redraw is easier to read.
tasks.hint: Would a sorted bar chart say it more clearly? Check that its axis starts at zero.
tasks.after: Delhi is third, with ₹1,05,593, after Mumbai (₹1,48,263) and Bengaluru (₹1,40,170). In a 10-slice 3D pie it is hard to rank, because people compare angles badly and the tilt makes front slices look bigger. A bar chart sorted largest first, with its axis starting at zero, shows the order at once.

reflection.prompt: Which number at your college, job or home would be worth tracking on a dashboard? What would you do differently if it went down?
reflection.hint: A good dashboard number leads to an action.

quiz.title: Is revenue rising?
quiz.scenario: A fertiliser dealer in Guntur has 18 months of revenue figures. The owner wants to see whether monthly revenue has risen, and whether it dips in the same months each year.
quiz.question: Which chart shows this best?
options: A line chart of revenue by month
A pie chart of revenue by month
A scatter plot of revenue by month
A bar chart sorted by revenue
quiz.explanation: Change over time is a line chart’s job. The months run left to right in order, so a rise, a fall or a yearly dip shows at once.
quiz.why_wrong: A pie shows parts of a whole and loses the order of the months; a scatter plot is for two measures that move together, and its separate dots make a trend harder to follow; sorting bars by revenue breaks the time order the owner needs.
quiz.learning_outcome: Use line charts for trends over time.

quiz.title: The giant jump
quiz.scenario: A Madurai jewellery chain’s bar chart shows this quarter’s sales at ₹52 lakh against ₹50 lakh last quarter. The new bar looks twice as tall as the old one.
quiz.question: What is most likely wrong?
options: The value axis starts near ₹48 lakh instead of zero, exaggerating a 4% rise
The data is wrong: a 4% rise can’t produce a bar that much taller
The bars are drawn in 3D, which makes the nearer bar look larger
The two quarters are measured in different units, so the bars can’t be compared directly
quiz.explanation: Readers judge bars by their length. With the axis starting at ₹48 lakh, the bars are 2 and 4 units tall, so a 4% rise looks like 100%. Bars must start at zero.
quiz.why_wrong: The numbers can be right while the drawing misleads; 3D can distort sizes a little, but it can’t double a bar; nothing suggests a units mix-up, and an axis starting at ₹48 lakh explains the doubling exactly.
quiz.learning_outcome: Start bar chart axes at zero.

quiz.title: The 30-minute promise
quiz.scenario: The operations head of a food-delivery company wants to see at a glance whether any city is missing its 30-minute delivery target.
quiz.question: What should the top of the dashboard show?
options: A table of every late order, so the head can read through the details
The national average delivery time, compared with last month
Total orders per city, since the busiest cities are the likeliest to be late
Each city’s on-time delivery % against the target, below-target cities highlighted
quiz.explanation: The question is “which city is off target?”, so the top shows that measure for each city with problems highlighted.
quiz.why_wrong: Every late order is too much detail; one national average hides which city is off target; busy cities aren’t necessarily the late ones.
quiz.learning_outcome: Design a dashboard around the decision it supports.

quiz.title: Two repeat rates
quiz.scenario: Copilot in Power BI drafts a measure, Repeat Customer Rate, that returns 74%. Your earlier SQL analysis found 41% for the same period.
quiz.question: What should you do first?
options: Publish Copilot’s figure, as it uses the live data model rather than an older query
Report both numbers side by side and let readers decide which to trust
Rerun your SQL until it matches Copilot, since the dashboard is what people see
Read the DAX it wrote, compare its definition and period with yours, then reconcile
quiz.explanation: Two methods disagreeing usually means two definitions. Reading the generated DAX shows what it actually calculates, so you can fix whichever is wrong.
quiz.why_wrong: Using the live model doesn’t make a definition right; two unexplained numbers confuse readers; forcing your SQL to match hides which definition is correct.
quiz.learning_outcome: Reconcile AI-drafted measures against a trusted result.

workbook.hook: A good dashboard tells a manager what to do next in five seconds.
idea: Pick the chart for the question: a line for change over time, a sorted bar for comparing categories, a scatter for two numbers together. Bars start at zero, and a pie gets only two or three slices.

A dashboard page answers three questions, top to bottom: are we on track, where is the problem, and what changed? Use colour only to point at what needs action, and check every number against a total you trust.
why: Managers decide in seconds, so the layout must do the work
The wrong chart can make a 2% gap look huge
Free tools (Looker Studio, Sheets charts, Power BI Desktop) are enough to build one
workbook.simple: A dashboard is like the one in a car. It shows speed and fuel up front, and lights up red only when something needs you. It doesn’t show every part of the engine.

myth.wrong: More charts make a better dashboard.
myth.right: Each page needs one purpose and the few numbers that serve it. Extra charts make people hunt for the one that matters.

example.title: The NGO’s four centres
example.body: Imagine Priya, who runs the office for an NGO’s 4 tuition centres in Kolkata. Her one-page dashboard has three parts. Top row: 280 students attending this month, against a target of 300. Middle: a sorted bar chart of attendance by centre, with the one centre below target in red. Bottom: a 12-week line of attendance. The director sees the red bar first and visits that centre on Monday.

terms.meaning: A number tracked against a target, such as orders this month.
One big number on a dashboard, often shown next to its target.
Bars in order from largest to smallest, for comparing categories.
Shows how a number changes over time.
An axis that doesn’t start at zero, which makes small gaps look big.
A Power BI formula that every chart reuses, so the number matches everywhere.

try_it.title: Ask AI to pick the chart
try_it.prompt: For each question, which chart should I use, and why? One line each. 1. How have a college’s monthly library visits changed over 2 years? 2. Which of 8 departments borrowed the most books this term? 3. What share of loans were print books and what share e-books? 4. Do students who borrow more books also attend more classes?
try_it.look_for: A line chart, a sorted bar chart, a pie or stacked bar with only two parts, and a scatter plot.
try_it.check: Match each answer to the first card’s list. If it suggests a pie for the 8 departments, ask it why a sorted bar wouldn’t be easier to compare.

try_it.title: See how an axis can mislead
try_it.prompt: A college fest sold these tickets: Day 1 420, Day 2 615, Day 3 380, Day 4 590. My bar chart’s axis starts at 350. How many times taller does Day 2’s bar look than Day 3’s, and how much more did Day 2 really sell? How do I fix the chart?
try_it.look_for: Day 2’s bar looks nearly 9 times as tall as Day 3’s, though Day 2 sold only about 62% more. The fix is to start the axis at zero.
try_it.check: Work it out: from 350, the bars are 265 and 30 units tall, and 265 ÷ 30 ≈ 8.8. From zero they are 615 and 380, and 615 ÷ 380 ≈ 1.6. Then chart the four days in Google Sheets (Insert > Chart) with the axis starting at 0.

workbook.tip: Show your page to someone who has never seen it, and ask what they look at first. It should be the most important number.
workbook.mistake: Giving every bar its own bright colour, so nothing stands out when one number really needs action.

checks.scenario: A school in Kozhikode wants to compare this year’s pass rates across its 7 subjects.
checks.question: Which chart suits this best?
options: A pie chart with one slice per subject
A line chart that joins up the 7 subjects
A bar chart sorted from highest to lowest
A scatter plot with a dot per subject
checks.hint: Is this change over time, parts of a whole, or a comparison of categories?
checks.why: Comparing categories calls for a sorted bar chart. Pass rates aren’t parts of one whole, so a pie doesn’t fit, a line suggests a change over time, and a scatter needs two numbers for each subject.

checks.scenario: Kiran has only an Android phone and a Google Sheet of her tea stall’s weekly sales. She wants a simple one-page chart view today, at no cost.
checks.question: Which should she use?
options: Power BI Desktop, which many employers use
Copilot in Power BI, to draft the page for her
Google Sheets charts, made on her phone
A DAX measure, so every chart uses one number
checks.hint: Which of the tools on the third card runs on a phone, for free?
checks.why: Sheets charts work on a phone and are enough for a simple one-page view. Power BI Desktop runs only on Windows computers, Copilot is a paid feature, and DAX is written inside Power BI.

checks.scenario: The founder of a Lucknow sweets chain asks you to add stock levels, staff rotas and Instagram followers to the one-page sales dashboard.
checks.question: What should you do?
options: Add them in small charts along the bottom row
Add them, but in grey so they draw less attention
Replace the trend line, the least-used chart
Give them their own pages, each with one purpose
checks.hint: What is this page for?
checks.why: The sales page answers whether sales are on track, where and what changed. Stock, rotas and followers are different questions, so each gets its own page. Squeezed in, greyed out or swapped for the trend, they crowd the sales story or remove part of it.

modules.title: AI as your analysis partner
modules.summary: Prompt free AI assistants well, check everything they produce against the data, and keep personal data safe.
modules.outcome: Use a free AI assistant to draft analysis, then check its output against the data before anyone relies on it.

learn.title: What AI is good at, and how to ask
learn.body:
AI assistants can draft SQL and pandas code from a plain-English question. They can explain a formula, suggest cleaning steps and propose charts. Free assistants such as ChatGPT, Claude and Gemini can all do this. Copilot in Excel and Power BI does too, on paid plans some employers provide.

They work best when you give them context. Worked example of a strong prompt:
“I use DuckDB. Table orders has order_id, order_date (a DATE), customer_id, order_value in ₹, and returned (1 or 0). Write a query for monthly revenue from kept orders (returned = 0) in 2026. One row per month, oldest first. Explain each line.”

It names the tool, the table, the columns, what they mean, and the output wanted. A weak prompt, “write SQL for monthly sales”, leaves the AI to guess all of that.

learn.title: Catch it before it costs you
learn.body:
AI can write code that runs but answers a different question. It can invent column names, mishandle dates or blanks, and state wrong numbers confidently. Treat its output like a new colleague’s first draft.

Worked example: a Kochi pharmacy asks for “monthly active customers”. The AI writes:
SELECT month, COUNT(customer_id) FROM orders GROUP BY month;
It runs. But COUNT(customer_id) counts orders, not people. You check 10 orders from one month by hand: 7 different customers placed them, but the query says 10. The fix:
SELECT month, COUNT(DISTINCT customer_id) FROM orders GROUP BY month;

Three checks catch most mistakes.
1. Run it on a small sample you can count by hand.
2. Compare a total with a source you trust.
3. Read the code for the definition: what exactly is counted?
Asking the same AI “is this right?” is not a check.

learn.title: Protect people’s data
learn.body:
Don’t paste personal data into public AI tools. That includes names, phone numbers, Aadhaar numbers and health details.

India’s Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 sets the rules. Personal data may be used only for a lawful purpose. That needs the person’s consent, or one of a few legitimate uses the Act lists. The data must also be kept safe. The DPDP Rules, 2025 bring in the duties in phases, and most apply to organisations from May 2027. Good practice starts now.

Worked example: you want AI help with a clinic’s appointments file. Use the tools your organisation approves. Otherwise, share only the column names and a made-up row:
patient_id, visit_date, department, fee
P001, 2026-05-02, ENT, 500
Then run the code the AI writes on the real data yourself.

tasks.title: Prompt, then check
tasks.prompt: Use any free AI assistant, such as ChatGPT, Claude or Gemini. Give it only the column names of Masala Mart’s orders.csv, not the data. Ask it for a DuckDB query that shows, for each month, the share of customers who were repeat customers. Define “repeat customer” in your prompt yourself. Run the query in shell.duckdb.org on orders.csv. Then run the three checks from the second card. Submit your prompt, the query, one month’s result, and what each check found.
tasks.hint: Decide first: is a repeat customer someone who ordered in an earlier month, or someone with 2 or more orders this month? The two give very different numbers.
tasks.after: A strong prompt names DuckDB, lists the column names and defines a repeat customer, for example “someone who also ordered in an earlier month”. The query runs on orders.csv. The three checks: count one month’s customers by hand on a small sample, compare a total (such as 2,030 orders or ₹7,55,512) with orders.csv, and read the code to see what it counts, such as COUNT(DISTINCT customer_id). “I asked the AI again” is not a check. With “a customer who also ordered in an earlier month”, April 2026 has 121 customers, 84 of them repeat: 69.4%. October 2025 shows 0%, since it is the first month in the file. Say so, rather than report it as a real figure.

tasks.title: Catch the error
tasks.prompt: An AI assistant read Masala Mart’s orders.csv and wrote: “Revenue grew 60% from Q1 to Q2 2026, driven by Bengaluru.” Check both parts against the data with a pivot table or SUMIFS in Google Sheets. Q1 is January to March and Q2 is April to June. Find the mistake, work out what the AI most likely did wrong, and rewrite the sentence correctly.
tasks.hint: Recalculate both quarters from the rows yourself. If your growth figure differs, try other date ranges to see which one gives 60%.
tasks.after: Q1 2026 (January to March) is ₹1,40,355 and Q2 (April to June) is ₹1,74,780: growth of about 24.5%, not 60%. The 60% comes from reading Q2 as April to July (₹2,24,785). The Bengaluru part holds: it added the most, about ₹10,243. A correct sentence: “Revenue grew about 25% from Q1 to Q2 2026, and Bengaluru added the most.”

reflection.prompt: Where would you trust an AI assistant fully, and where would you always check its work? Why the difference?
reflection.hint: Think about the cost of a mistake in each case.

quiz.title: Average fare per route
quiz.scenario: A bus-booking app keeps its data in DuckDB, in a table bookings(booking_id, user_id, route, booked_at, fare). The operations head wants the average fare on each route for October 2026.
quiz.question: Which prompt is most likely to get correct SQL from an AI assistant?
options: “Write SQL for the average fares on my bus booking app last month. Make it efficient and easy to read.”
“DuckDB. Table bookings(booking_id, user_id, route, booked_at, fare): average fare per route, October 2026, highest first.”
“You are an expert data analyst with 20 years of experience. Analyse my bus booking data and tell me everything about fares.”
“Using my company database, work out the average fare for each route last month and draw it as a bar chart.”
quiz.explanation: It names the tool, the table and its columns, the measure, the period and the order of the output. The assistant has nothing to guess.
quiz.why_wrong: “Make it efficient” gives no table, columns or exact period, so the assistant must invent them; the expert persona names neither the table nor the measure; “my company database” gives the assistant no schema to work from.
quiz.learning_outcome: Give AI the schema, the definition and the goal.

quiz.title: Code that runs
quiz.scenario: AI-written pandas code runs without errors and reports an average order value of ₹1,240.
quiz.question: What is the best way to check it?
options: Work out the same figure another way for a month you know, such as with a PivotTable
Trust it: code that runs on the full file without errors has been checked by Python
Ask the assistant to double-check its own code and confirm the figure
Compare it with last year’s average order value; if it’s close, it’s right
quiz.explanation: An independent calculation is the only real check: code can run perfectly and still compute the wrong thing.
quiz.why_wrong: Running without errors says nothing about correctness; the assistant checking itself isn’t independent; last year’s figure can’t confirm this year’s calculation.
quiz.learning_outcome: Verify AI output with an independent calculation.

quiz.title: The patient list
quiz.scenario: You want an AI assistant’s help cleaning a list of 20,000 patients with names, phone numbers and diagnoses.
quiz.question: What is the right approach?
options: Paste the whole file into a free AI chatbot, since it deletes conversations once you close the window
Remove the diagnosis column first, then share the names and phone numbers, which aren’t sensitive
Use an approved tool, or share only the column names and made-up rows and run the code yourself
Replace names with initials, keep the phones and diagnoses, and paste it into a free chatbot
quiz.explanation: Personal and health data must stay within approved systems. Sharing the structure with made-up rows gets the help without exposing anyone.
quiz.why_wrong: You can’t be sure a free chatbot doesn’t keep what you paste; names and phone numbers are personal data on their own; initials don’t hide anyone while phone numbers and diagnoses stay.
quiz.learning_outcome: Never share personal data with unapproved AI tools.

quiz.title: The column that isn’t there
quiz.scenario: AI-written SQL refers to a column customers.lifetime_value, which doesn’t exist in your database.
quiz.question: What does this tell you?
options: The database is missing a column the query needs, so ask IT to add lifetime_value to the table
It guessed your schema: give it the real table definitions and re-check the whole query
Create the column and fill it with sample values so the query can run
Remove that line; if the rest of the query runs, its result can be trusted
quiz.explanation: An invented column shows the assistant was guessing, so other parts may be guesses too. Supply the schema and re-check everything.
quiz.why_wrong: lifetime_value was invented, not missing; filling it with made-up values corrupts the result; a query that runs can still be wrong.
quiz.learning_outcome: An invented detail means: re-check the whole answer.

workbook.hook: AI drafts your query in seconds. Checking it is your job.
idea: Free assistants such as ChatGPT, Claude and Gemini can draft SQL and pandas, explain formulas and suggest charts. Tell them the tool, the table, the columns, what the columns mean, and the output you want.

AI code can run and still answer a different question. Test it on a small sample you can count by hand, compare a total with a source you trust, and read exactly what it counts. Never paste personal data into a public AI tool.
why: Drafting code with AI saves time on routine queries
A wrong number you share is your mistake, not the AI’s
India’s DPDP Act, 2023 sets rules for using people’s personal data
workbook.simple: AI is like a quick new intern. It finishes in minutes and sounds sure of itself. You still check the work before your name goes on it.

myth.wrong: Asking the AI “Are you sure?” is a good way to check its answer.
myth.right: The same AI may simply agree, or change a right answer. A real check uses something outside it: a hand count, a trusted total, or reading the code yourself.

example.title: The homestay’s nights
example.body: Imagine Tara, who analyses bookings for a homestay in Goa. She tells a free AI: “I use DuckDB. Table stays has stay_id, guest_id, check_in (a DATE) and nights. Write a query for the nights booked each month in 2026.” It returns SUM(nights) grouped by month. She checks March by hand on 10 rows, then compares the year’s total with the owner’s register. Both match, so she shares it.

terms.meaning: What you tell the AI: the tool, the table, the columns and the output you want.
A confident answer the AI made up, such as a column that doesn’t exist.
Running the code on a few rows you can count by hand.
Counts different values, such as different customers, not rows.
Anything that identifies a person: a name, phone number, Aadhaar number or health details.
A fake row that shows the AI the shape of your data without real details.

try_it.title: Write a prompt with full context
try_it.prompt: I use pandas. DataFrame df has ticket_id, show_date (already dates), seat_type ('Gold' or 'Silver') and price in ₹. Write code for the total ticket revenue by seat type in March 2026, largest first. Explain each line.
try_it.look_for: A filter with & and brackets on show_date, then groupby("seat_type")["price"].sum() and a sort, largest first.
try_it.check: In Colab, make 5 rows yourself, including one on 31 March and one on 1 April. Total each seat type by hand first. If the 1 April row is counted, or the 31 March row is missed, the date filter is wrong.

try_it.title: Catch a counting mistake
try_it.prompt: Here are 8 orders as customer_id and month: C1 Jan, C2 Jan, C1 Jan, C3 Jan, C2 Feb, C2 Feb, C4 Feb, C1 Feb. Write SQL for monthly active customers from a table orders(customer_id, month), and give me the result for each month.
try_it.look_for: COUNT(DISTINCT customer_id), and 3 customers in each month, not 4.
try_it.check: Count by hand: January has 4 orders from 3 people, because C1 ordered twice. If the AI says 4, it counted orders. Tell it which step is wrong, rather than asking “are you sure?”.

workbook.tip: Keep a made-up row for each table you use often. Paste it with the column names, and the AI writes better code without seeing real data.
workbook.mistake: Pasting a real customer list into a public AI tool to “clean it quickly”.

checks.scenario: An AI writes a query for “patients each month” at a Nagpur dental clinic. It returns SUM(visits) for each month.
checks.question: Which check catches the problem fastest?
options: Compare the year’s total with the appointment book
Run it again and see if the number changes
Read the code to see what it adds up
Ask the AI whether its query is right
checks.hint: Which check can you do in seconds, with no other data?
checks.why: Reading the code shows at once that it adds visits, so a patient who comes 3 times counts 3 times. Comparing with the appointment book would also catch it, but only after you total the book. Running it again gives the same wrong number, and asking the same AI is not a check.

checks.scenario: A query counts the people who used a college gym in May. 5 students came 4 times each, and nobody else came.
checks.question: What should COUNT(DISTINCT student_id) return?
checks.hint: What does DISTINCT do to repeats?
checks.why: 5 different students came, so COUNT(DISTINCT student_id) is 5. 20 is the number of visits, which COUNT(student_id) would give, and 4 is how often each came.

checks.scenario: A coaching centre in Patna collected parents’ phone numbers at admission. It now wants to send them fee reminders by SMS.
checks.question: Under the DPDP Act, 2023, what makes this use lawful?
options: Nothing more: a stored number can be used for any purpose
A separate signed consent form for every reminder it sends
Registering the centre with the Data Protection Board first
Consent for it, or a legitimate use the Act lists
checks.hint: What does the Act say every use of personal data needs?
checks.why: The Act allows personal data to be used only for a lawful purpose: the person’s consent, or one of the legitimate uses it lists. Storing a number gives no right to use it for anything. Consent covers a stated purpose, so it isn’t needed again for each reminder, and the Act has no step of registering an ordinary business with the Data Protection Board.

modules.title: From numbers to decisions
modules.summary: Lead with the recommendation, turn findings into actions, and be honest about limits.
modules.outcome: Write a recommendation a manager can act on from its first two lines, with the evidence and its honest limits.

learn.title: Lead with the answer
learn.body:
Most managers read the first two lines, then decide whether to read on. So start with the recommendation and the number behind it.

Before: “This report analyses six months of marketing data from January to June 2026 across two channels.”
After: “Move ₹2 lakh a month from Meta ads to Google Search in Pune. Search brings in a customer for ₹310, against ₹780 on Meta.”

What changed? The action comes first. It names the amount, the place and the channel. The one number that justifies it comes next. After that come the evidence and then the limits.

The common mistake is telling the story of your work in the order you did it. The manager needs the decision, not your journey.

learn.title: So what, and now what?
learn.body:
For every chart, say what it shows and what it means for the decision. A finding says what the data shows. An insight says why it matters. An action says what to do next.

Worked example from a Nagpur bookshop:
- Finding: weekend sales are 40% of the week’s sales, but the same 2 staff work every day.
- Insight: at weekends customers wait at the counter, and some leave without buying.
- Action: add a part-time staff member at weekends for a month. Then compare weekend sales with last month.

The action is small, specific and testable. “Improve the weekend experience” is not an action, because nobody knows what to do on Monday.

Write job titles and terms in full the first time: finance head (CFO), cash on delivery (COD).

learn.title: Be honest about uncertainty
learn.body:
State the period, the data source, the sample size and what you couldn’t check. A recommendation with clear limits earns more trust than a confident one that later falls apart.

Worked example: a one-line caveat under a skincare brand’s recommendation.
“Based on 14,000 customers, January to June 2026. Customers chose the trial kit themselves, so keen buyers may have picked it. A 4-week A/B test would confirm it.”

That line does three jobs. It says how much data there is. It names the main doubt: people chose for themselves (you met this in the first module and the statistics module). And it says what would settle the doubt.

The common mistake is hiding limits in a footnote, or leaving them out. If your manager finds a limit you didn’t mention, they stop trusting the rest.

tasks.title: Write the memo opening
tasks.prompt: In Module 2 (Spreadsheets that answer questions) you found Masala Mart’s return rate by payment method (orders.csv, October 2025 to September 2026). Cash on delivery (COD) orders are returned far more often than UPI or card orders. Assume each return costs the brand about ₹90 in shipping both ways. Write the first paragraph of a memo to the founder: your recommendation first, the numbers behind it, and one honest caveat.
tasks.hint: Recommendation first, evidence second, one caveat. Did customers choose how to pay? What would a test show?
tasks.after: A strong opening starts with the action, for example: “Test a small fee or a prepaid discount on cash-on-delivery orders for a month.” Then the numbers: COD orders are returned 17.3% of the time, against 5.3% for UPI and 3.9% for cards, and the year’s 91 COD returns cost about ₹8,190 at ₹90 each. Then the caveat: customers chose how to pay, so a test would show whether nudging them really cuts returns.

tasks.title: Turn findings into actions
tasks.prompt: Three findings from a college canteen’s sales data: 60% of sales happen between 12:30 and 1:30 pm; the queue takes 14 minutes at peak; 30% of students who arrive at peak leave without buying. Write one insight and one action for each finding.
tasks.hint: What could the canteen change by next week? Make each action small enough to test.
tasks.after: Each line goes beyond the number. Lunch peak: the canteen gets most sales in one hour, so pre-pack the 3 best-selling meals before 12:30 for two weeks. 14-minute queue: students with short breaks can’t wait that long, so open a second till from 12:30 to 1:30 and time the queue again. 30% leaving: those are customers already at the counter, so try a pre-order counter for a week and count how many still leave.

reflection.prompt: Think of a presentation or message that persuaded you. What did the person do that you could use in your own reports?
reflection.hint: Notice what came first, and what they left out.

quiz.title: Two minutes with the operations head
quiz.scenario: You analysed a year of returns for an Agra footwear brand that sells online. The operations head has two minutes before a meeting and will read only your first line.
quiz.question: Which opening line should you send?
options: “Recommendation: offer free size exchanges instead of refunds; size returns cost us about ₹4 lakh a month.”
“This report analyses 14 tables and 2.1 million rows from our order, return and payment systems.”
“Data was collected from several sources over twelve months and cleaned with a documented process.”
“Here are 25 charts covering sales, returns, exchanges and payments, organised by region, by store and by month.”
quiz.explanation: It leads with an action and the money behind it, so the head can decide in the two minutes available. The evidence and the limits can follow.
quiz.why_wrong: The count of tables and rows says how big the work was, not what to do; how the data was collected is method, which belongs lower down; 25 charts leave the reader to find the point alone.
quiz.learning_outcome: Lead with the recommendation and its impact.

quiz.title: The weekly update
quiz.scenario: An analyst at a Mysuru online furniture store drafts four lines for the weekly update to the founder.
quiz.question: Which line is an insight with an action, not just a finding?
options: “The average order value is ₹6,400, slightly higher than in the same month last year.”
“40% of carts are dropped at the delivery fee; show it on product pages for a month and compare.”
“We now have 12,000 customers, most in Maharashtra and Karnataka, up from 9,000 last year.”
“Sales were higher in October, when the festive season began across the country.”
quiz.explanation: It links a specific problem, carts dropped at the delivery fee, to a likely cause. It also names a small change and a way to test it.
quiz.why_wrong: ₹6,400 against last year is a finding with no “so what”; the customer count by state is growth with no action attached; linking October sales to the festive season explains a finding but says nothing to do next.
quiz.learning_outcome: Turn findings into insights by adding “so what” and “now what”.

quiz.title: Festive data
quiz.scenario: Your analysis of a jewellery brand’s website rests on three weeks of data, all during Diwali.
quiz.question: What should your memo say about it?
options: Nothing: mentioning limits would make the reader doubt the whole analysis
That the results are certain, because the festive weeks have the most orders of the whole year
That it covers only three festive weeks, which may not reflect a normal month, so re-check it
Remove the festive weeks, and say there isn’t yet enough normal-month data to report anything
quiz.explanation: Saying what the data covers, and when to check again, lets the reader act sensibly on the result.
quiz.why_wrong: Hiding a limit misleads; festive weeks aren’t typical of the rest of the year; withholding the results helps no one.
quiz.learning_outcome: State the limits of your data and how to address them.

quiz.title: Did the loyalty programme pay?
quiz.scenario: The chief financial officer (CFO) of a Pune supermarket chain asks whether the loyalty programme it launched six months ago has paid for itself.
quiz.question: Which answer is most useful?
options: “Yes: engagement is up across app opens, product reviews and referrals in the six months since the launch.”
“Yes: members spent ₹38 lakh more than shoppers who aren’t members over six months, so it has clearly paid off.”
“Yes: members spent ₹38 lakh more than similar shoppers who didn’t join; it cost ₹22 lakh, so ₹16 lakh net.”
“It’s too early to say; loyalty programmes usually take a year to show results.”
quiz.explanation: It answers in money, subtracts the cost, and compares members with similar shoppers who didn’t join, because keen shoppers spent more even before they joined.
quiz.why_wrong: Engagement doesn’t answer a money question; comparing members with all non-members ignores that keen shoppers already spent more, and leaves out the cost; six months of data can already answer it.
quiz.learning_outcome: Answer the question asked, in its own terms.

workbook.hook: Your analysis only counts if someone acts on it. Make the first line do that.
idea: Lead with the answer: the recommendation, then the one number behind it, then the evidence and the limits. Many managers read only the first two lines.
Turn each finding into an insight (why it matters) and an action (what to do next) that is small, specific and testable. State the period, the data, the sample size and what you couldn’t check.
why: A clear first line gets read and acted on
A specific action can be tested and measured
Honest limits make people trust the rest
workbook.simple: It’s like a cricket captain at the toss. He doesn’t read out the pitch report first. He says “We’ll bowl”, and gives the reason if he’s asked.

myth.wrong: Admitting the limits of your analysis makes you look weak.
myth.right: A clear caveat earns trust. If a manager finds a limit you hid, they stop trusting everything else.

example.title: The textile shop’s queue
example.body: Vikram, an intern at a textile shop in Surat, writes a first draft that starts, “I looked at 9 months of sales across 3 counters.” He rewrites it: “Open the second billing counter on Saturdays from 5 to 8 pm. Saturday evening queues average 18 minutes, and 1 in 5 customers leaves without buying.” Then come the evidence and one caveat: the queues were timed by hand on 6 Saturdays.

terms.meaning: The action you advise, stated first.
What the data shows.
Why the finding matters for the decision.
A small, specific, testable step someone can start next week.
A short, honest note of what the analysis can’t show.

try_it.title: Put the answer first
try_it.prompt: Rewrite this opening so the recommendation comes first, then the number behind it, in under 50 words: “This note reviews three months of data from our two college canteens, covering 9,000 bills. We compared menus, prices and timings. Canteen B sells 35% more breakfast than Canteen A, and B opens at 7:30 am while A opens at 8:30 am.”
try_it.look_for: A first line that is an action, such as opening Canteen A at 7:30 am for a month as a trial, followed by the 35% gap.
try_it.check: Read only the first line: could a manager act on it? Also check the AI doesn’t claim the opening time causes the gap. The two only go together; a one-month trial would test it.

try_it.title: Write a one-line caveat
try_it.prompt: Students who used a free online practice test scored 11 marks higher in the final exam. The data covers 600 students from one college in one semester, and students chose whether to take the practice test. Write a one-line caveat, under 40 words, that names the sample, the main doubt and what would settle it.
try_it.look_for: The 600 students and the one semester, the doubt that keener students chose the practice test, and a random trial to settle it.
try_it.check: Tick the three jobs from the third card: how much data, the main doubt, and what would settle it. If the line says the practice test “caused” the higher marks, ask the AI to remove that claim.

workbook.tip: Before you send, cover everything but your first two lines. If they don’t say what to do and why, rewrite them.
workbook.mistake: Writing the action as a hope, such as “improve the customer experience”, which nobody can start on Monday.

checks.scenario: A note on a bookstore’s data ends: “Put a second till on Saturday afternoons for four weeks, then compare sales with last month.”
checks.question: What kind of statement is this?
options: A finding, since it says what the data shows
An insight, since it says why the data matters
A caveat, since it says what can’t be checked
An action, since it says what to do next
checks.hint: Does it describe, explain, warn, or tell someone what to do?
checks.why: It tells the store what to do and how to test it, so it is an action. A finding reports the data, an insight explains why it matters, and a caveat names a limit.

checks.scenario: A hostel mess finds that 40% of the dinner it cooks on Sundays is thrown away.
checks.question: Which is the best action?
options: Cook 40% less every day for a week
Cook 30% less on Sundays for 4 weeks, then compare
Survey 30 students about Sunday dinner, then decide
Ask students to be more careful about food waste
checks.hint: Where was the waste found, and how would you know a change worked?
checks.why: Cooking 30% less on Sundays for 4 weeks is small, specific and testable: weigh the waste and see. The finding is about Sundays, not every day, a survey delays acting on a clear finding, and “being more careful” isn’t a step anyone can measure.

checks.scenario: Anjali’s recommendation to a salon rests on a survey that 25 regular customers filled in at the counter.
checks.question: Which caveat should go beside it?
options: Based on 25 regulars; new customers may differ.
Based on 25 customers; a bigger survey would settle it.
Based on 25 regulars; results may change next year.
Filled in at the counter; staff may have helped.
checks.hint: Think about who filled in the survey, and who never saw it.
checks.why: It states the sample (25 regulars) and the main doubt: newer customers weren’t asked. A bigger survey at the same counter would still ask only regulars, next year is not the doubt, and the last one leaves out how much data there is.

questions.title: Is marketing working?
questions.scenario: Hamsa runs marketing for a Bhubaneswar snack brand that sells online. From April to June she spent ₹6 lakh on Instagram ads and ₹6 lakh on Google ads. She asks you, “Is our marketing working?” She must set next quarter’s budget by Friday.
questions.question: Which version of her question can an analysis actually answer?
options: “Did Q2 Instagram customers cost less per first order than Google ones, and should budget move?”
“Are our Instagram and Google campaigns working, judging by the likes, clicks and reach they got in Q2?”
“What are all our marketing numbers for the last year, by channel and by month?”
“Do customers like our ads, and which of them do they remember best?”
questions.explanation: It names the channels, the period (Q2), one measure (cost per first order) and the decision it feeds (moving budget). So the data can answer it before Friday.
questions.why_wrong: Likes, clicks and reach measure attention, not whether the ads bring paying customers; every number by month answers no particular question; whether customers like or remember ads needs a survey and points to no decision.
questions.learning_outcome: A question becomes answerable when it names a measure, a period and a decision.

questions.title: The red stores
questions.scenario: A Tiruchirappalli grocery chain’s dashboard turns a store red on any day its sales fall below ₹68,000. Store 12’s daily sales have been between ₹60,000 and ₹80,000 for 60 days. So it turns red on many ordinary days, and managers now ignore the colour.
questions.question: Which change would make the red flag most useful?
options: Flag a store when its 7-day average falls below its own usual range, not on one low day
Lower the red line to ₹55,000 for every store, so that the flag appears much less often
Drop the colour and show every store’s daily sales in a table, so managers judge for themselves
Turn a store red whenever today’s sales are below yesterday’s, to catch every drop early
questions.explanation: Store 12’s sales normally swing between ₹60,000 and ₹80,000, so one low day is noise. Comparing a 7-day average with the store’s own usual range flags a real fall and keeps red meaningful.
questions.why_wrong: One line for every store ignores each store’s own normal level, so a big store could fall a long way before turning red; a table removes the at-a-glance signal the dashboard exists for; comparing with yesterday turns ordinary daily swings red even more often.
questions.learning_outcome: Set alerts against normal variation, not single values.

questions.title: The SKUs that won’t match
questions.scenario: A Vijayawada wholesaler copies SKUs from suppliers’ PDF invoices into a sheet. It uses =XLOOKUP(B2, Master[SKU], Master[Category], "New SKU"). 300 of 4,000 lines show “New SKU”, but when you search the master by eye, those SKUs are there.
questions.question: What is the most likely cause?
options: The master isn’t sorted A to Z, and XLOOKUP needs sorted data to find an exact match
Some copied SKUs carry hidden spaces, so they aren’t exactly equal to the master’s
XLOOKUP is doing an approximate match, because the fourth argument wasn’t set to exact
Those 300 SKUs really are new, so add them to the master and run the lookup again
questions.explanation: A lookup matches only identical values. A SKU copied with a space before or after it looks the same on screen but doesn’t match. Trim the column, then check that the count of “New SKU” falls.
questions.why_wrong: XLOOKUP’s exact match works on unsorted data; its fourth argument is the not-found value, and its default match is already exact; the SKUs are already in the master, so adding them again creates duplicates and leaves the real cause in place.
questions.learning_outcome: When a lookup fails on values that look equal, check for hidden spaces.

questions.title: The AI’s cleaning step
questions.scenario: A Shillong music school has 9,400 trial-class sign-ups (student_name, phone, instrument, signup_date). An AI assistant suggests df = df.drop_duplicates(subset="student_name") to remove repeat sign-ups. After it runs, 7,100 rows are left.
questions.question: What should you do before keeping the result?
options: Look at some removed rows: students can share a name, so match on name and phone
Keep it, because the code ran without errors and repeat sign-ups are very common
Ask the assistant whether 7,100 is the right count, and keep it if it agrees
Run drop_duplicates() with no subset instead, so it catches every repeated sign-up
questions.explanation: Dropping duplicates on name alone treats every student with the same name as one person, so real students disappear. Looking at the removed rows shows the problem, and matching on name and phone together keeps different people apart.
questions.why_wrong: Code that runs can still remove the wrong rows; the assistant checking its own number isn’t an independent check; with no subset, only rows identical in every column go, so repeat sign-ups on different dates stay.
questions.learning_outcome: Check what an AI-written cleaning step removed before you trust it.

questions.title: The income question
questions.scenario: An NGO in Ranchi surveys 800 households about their monthly income. 240 of them (30%) leave the income question blank. You are asked to report the average income.
questions.question: What is the best practice?
options: Fill the blanks with 0, so that every respondent is included in the average income
Fill each blank with the average of those who answered, so the sample size isn’t reduced
Report the average for those who answered, the share missing, and whether skippers differ
Report the average of those who answered, without mentioning the blanks
questions.explanation: A blank is unknown, not zero. Saying who is included, how many are missing, and whether the households that skipped look different keeps the average honest.
questions.why_wrong: Filling blanks with 0 invents zero incomes and drags the average down; filling with the average hides the gap and makes the result look more certain than it is; staying silent about 30% missing hides a limit the reader needs.
questions.learning_outcome: Report who is missing from an average, and whether they differ.

questions.title: Big payments by method
questions.scenario: A bill-payment app in Visakhapatnam keeps a payments table with payment_id, method (UPI, card or net banking) and amount in ₹. An analyst runs: SELECT method, COUNT(*) FROM payments WHERE amount > 1000 GROUP BY method;
questions.question: What does the result show?
options: The total amount paid above ₹1,000, for each payment method
The payment methods that have more than 1,000 payments
The average payment for each method, for payments over ₹1,000
The number of payments above ₹1,000 for each method
questions.explanation: WHERE keeps only payments above ₹1,000. GROUP BY method then makes one group per method, and COUNT(*) counts the payments in each.
questions.why_wrong: COUNT(*) counts payments, it doesn’t add their amounts; the 1,000 filters each payment’s amount, not the number of payments; COUNT gives a count, not an average.
questions.learning_outcome: Read WHERE as a row filter and COUNT(*) as a count per group.

questions.title: The pivot table that won’t add up
questions.scenario: A Tiruppur garment wholesaler pastes 6,000 order lines into Google Sheets and builds a pivot table of order_value by city. It shows a count of order_value, and switching to SUM gives 0 for every city. The order_value column holds entries like “Rs 1,250/-” and “Rs 980/-”.
questions.question: What should you do so the pivot table shows each city’s total?
options: Change the pivot table’s summary from SUM to AVERAGE, which works on text and numbers alike
Format the order_value column as Currency (₹), so the sheet reads it as money
Convert order_value to numbers (remove Rs, commas and /-), then refresh the pivot table
Add order_value to Rows as well as Values, so each amount is shown separately
questions.explanation: SUM skips text, and “Rs 1,250/-” is text, not a number. Once the column holds real numbers, the pivot table can add it up for each city.
questions.why_wrong: AVERAGE skips text too, so it fails in the same way; a currency format changes how a number looks but doesn’t turn text into a number; putting the amount in Rows lists each value instead of totalling it.
questions.learning_outcome: A pivot table can only add a column stored as numbers.

questions.title: Months when orders fell
questions.scenario: A quick-commerce dark store in Navi Mumbai keeps a table monthly_orders(month, orders), with one row per month. The manager wants the months in which orders fell compared with the month before.
questions.question: Which query lists those months?
options: WITH m AS (SELECT month, orders, LAG(orders) OVER (ORDER BY month) AS prev FROM monthly_orders) SELECT month FROM m WHERE orders < prev;
SELECT month FROM monthly_orders WHERE orders < LAG(orders) OVER (ORDER BY month);
WITH m AS (SELECT month, orders, LEAD(orders) OVER (ORDER BY month) AS prev FROM monthly_orders) SELECT month FROM m WHERE orders < prev;
WITH m AS (SELECT month, orders, LAG(orders) OVER (PARTITION BY month ORDER BY month) AS prev FROM monthly_orders) SELECT month FROM m WHERE orders < prev;
questions.explanation: LAG(orders) OVER (ORDER BY month) puts the previous month’s orders on each row. A window function can’t go in WHERE. So the WITH step works it out first, and the outer query keeps the months where orders < prev.
questions.why_wrong: A window function in WHERE stops with an error, because WHERE runs before windows are worked out; LEAD brings in the next month, so the query lists the months just before a rise, not the months that fell; PARTITION BY month makes each month its own window, so prev is always NULL and no month is listed.
questions.learning_outcome: Use LAG in a WITH step, then filter, to compare each period with the one before.

questions.title: Two figures for spending
questions.scenario: A survey of 2,000 households in Anand district, Gujarat, finds median monthly spending of ₹18,000 and mean spending of ₹31,000.
questions.question: What does the gap between the two figures suggest?
options: Spending is spread evenly, and most households spend about ₹31,000
The data must contain errors, since the median and the mean should be close
Most households spend more than ₹31,000, and a few spend very little
A few households with very high spending pull the mean above the median
questions.explanation: When the mean is far above the median, a small number of large values is pulling it up. Half the households spend ₹18,000 or less, so ₹31,000 isn’t typical.
questions.why_wrong: Even spending would put the mean and the median close together; a gap between them is normal when a few values are very large, not a sign of errors; if most households spent more than ₹31,000, the median would be above ₹31,000.
questions.learning_outcome: A mean well above the median signals a few very large values.

questions.title: A 0.1-point lead
questions.scenario: A train-ticket app is testing a new booking button. So far, version A converts 4.0% of 50,000 visitors and version B converts 4.1% of 50,000. The test has run 5 of its planned 14 days.
questions.question: What should you do before calling B the winner?
options: Declare B the winner, since 50,000 visitors per version is plenty of data for a clear result
Run the test again in a single city, to see whether B wins there too
Check the gap against chance with an A/B test calculator, and run all 14 days
Add a third version, C, to see whether the gap between them grows
questions.explanation: 4.0% and 4.1% of 50,000 are 2,000 and 2,050 conversions, a gap well within chance. An A/B test calculator would show this, and stopping on day 5 risks crowning a lucky early lead.
questions.why_wrong: A large sample can still show a gap that chance explains, and 0.1 points is tiny; one city shrinks the sample and makes chance bigger; adding version C changes the test without checking A against B.
questions.learning_outcome: A small gap needs checking against chance, over the planned run, before you name a winner.

questions.title: The checkout test, city by city
